sections.overview: The Mallard is a widespread Northern Hemisphere duck of wetlands, farms and city ponds. Its success comes from a flexible diet, broad tolerance of shallow waters and the ability of many populations to remain near open water through winter. In North America, adults typically measure 50–65 cm long with an 82–95 cm wingspan; the sexes are similar in size, usually weighing 0.9–1.4 kg. Those measurements describe the species, while regional populations and individual condition cause variation.
sections.identification: The adult male is unmistakable in breeding plumage: an iridescent green head, narrow white neck ring, chestnut breast, grey body and curled black tail feathers. The female is mottled brown, with a dark eye-line and orange-and-black bill; her patterned plumage blends into nesting cover. Both sexes show a blue-violet speculum bordered by white, visible when the wing opens. After breeding, the male moults into a dull, female-like eclipse plumage while replacing his flight feathers, leaving him temporarily flightless; a later moult restores bright colours. Adults are about 50–65 cm long, with an 82–95 cm wingspan. British ringing measurements average 1,270 g for males and 1,130 g for females; these are population averages, and body mass varies seasonally. No useful height or body-width measurement was found.
sections.habitat: Mallards favour shallow, sheltered water: marshes, ponds, small lakes, estuaries and flooded fields provide feeding areas and nearby cover. They also graze on land, including stubble fields, and readily use artificial ponds and urban parks. Nests are usually on dry ground in grass or other dense vegetation, often some distance from water; after hatching, the female leads the brood from the nest to water. This combination of wet feeding habitat and undisturbed nesting cover matters more than any single plant community. In the Prairie Pothole Region of North America, small seasonal wetlands are especially important breeding and brood-rearing sites.
sections.diet: A broad, flattened bill fringed with comb-like lamellae lets the Mallard strain edible particles from water and mud. It usually feeds by dabbling at the surface or tipping forward to reach submerged plants and invertebrates, rather than pursuing prey underwater. Water and food move through the bill; the lamellae retain particles as water and fine debris drain away. Seeds, aquatic vegetation, insects, worms, snails and crustaceans all occur in the diet, whose balance changes with season and local supply. On land, it takes grain and other plant foods, then returns to water to rinse and separate indigestible material from a food bolus.
sections.behavior: Outside nesting, Mallards gather in flocks and feed or rest together, while pairs form well before eggs are laid. Courtship uses head bobs, calls and chases; females give the loud quack, males a quieter rasp. Many northern birds migrate south as wetlands freeze, but movements vary: some populations are resident, and others mix residents with seasonal visitors.
sections.reproduction: Pairs commonly form in autumn or winter, months before breeding, and are generally seasonal rather than lifelong. The female makes a shallow, grass-lined ground nest, adds down from her breast, and lays a clutch usually numbering about 11–14 eggs in British records. She alone incubates for roughly 27–28 days; the male leaves to join other males. Ducklings hatch covered in down, leave the nest soon after hatching and swim and feed themselves under the female’s guidance. They are precocial, but remain vulnerable to predators and depend on their mother for protection and access to suitable feeding wetlands. They typically fledge at 50–60 days. Mallards generally reach reproductive maturity at about one year.
sections.ecology: Feeding on aquatic vegetation, seeds, invertebrates and crops makes Mallards consumers of plant production and small animal prey across wetlands and farmland. Their broad bill and opportunistic diet overlap with those of other dabbling ducks; prey size and the amount of detritus can alter how much food each species filters from the same water. Aquatic invertebrates are especially important to growing ducklings, and field experiments in North American prairie wetlands linked greater invertebrate abundance with faster early growth. Eggs and young are prey for mammals, birds, reptiles and fish, so dense cover and productive brood wetlands affect survival. Mallards also hybridize with related ducks; releases of farm-reared Mallards have introduced domestic ancestry into some wild populations, documented in Europe and North America.
sections.conservation: BirdLife International’s global IUCN assessment dated 5 June 2025 lists the Mallard as Least Concern, while recording a decreasing population trend. That global category reflects the species’ enormous range and population; it does not mean every regional population is stable. North American monitoring and management have long tracked breeding numbers, habitat conditions and harvest, while wetland availability remains important to nesting and brood survival. A separate, well-documented pressure comes from releasing farm-reared birds: genomic studies identify ongoing domestic introgression in parts of Europe and North America. The species is also the ancestor of most domestic duck breeds, so feral and farm-origin birds can complicate local conservation of closely related wild ducks.
